eligibility.exact_action_basis: H.R.29 would extend the federal mandatory-custody category to the following offenses: burglary, theft, larceny or shoplifting. The four listed property-offense terms take the meaning assigned by the jurisdiction where the acts occurred. The exact bill adds an INA 236(c) mandatory-custody category requiring inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(6)(A), (6)(C), or (7) together with a specified criminal predicate: being charged, arrested, convicted, admitting commission, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements. These inadmissibility categories concern presence without admission/parole or undesignated arrival, material immigration fraud/false citizenship claims, and specified entry-document defects, subject to their existing statutory qualifications. DHS must issue a detainer for a person meeting the new ground and, if the person is not otherwise detained by Federal, State or local officials, effectively and expeditiously take custody. The bill also gives a State attorney general or other authorized State officer standing, on alleged harm to the State or residents (including financial harm in excess of $100), to seek appropriate injunctive relief in district court over five specified federal matters: INA 235(b)(1)/(2) detention/removal requirements; INA 236 release, bond or parole decisions; the existing INA 243(d) visa-discontinuance requirement for countries denying or unreasonably delaying acceptance; violation of the existing INA 212(d)(5)(A) case-by-case urgent-humanitarian/significant-public-benefit parole limits; and INA 241(a)(2) detention during the removal period. Courts must advance and expedite these cases to the greatest practicable extent. INA 236(e) removes its express release/grant shield while leaving the other printed discretionary-judgment/detention/revocation/denial restrictions, and INA 242(f)(1) receives an exception for the printed listed actions, while its separate final-removal-order injunction standard remains. These review changes do not establish a general right to enjoin every immigration action. The parole clause changes its named administering actor to the Secretary of Homeland Security. The baseline removal period is generally 90 days with specified starting/extension conditions; the bill adds litigation standing over its detention requirement rather than creating that period. The pre-existing narrow witness/cooperator-protection release exception remains, redesignated as INA 236(c)(4).

The exact House-passed H.R.23 requires the President, not later than 60 days after enactment and on an ongoing basis, to impose sanctions if the ICC is attempting to investigate, arrest, detain or prosecute a protected person. Covered foreign persons are those the President determines directly engage in or aid such an effort; materially assist, sponsor or provide specified support/goods/services for it; or are owned/controlled by, or currently act or purport to have acted for, a person directly engaging in it. For covered aliens, the bill makes them inadmissible, ineligible for visas or other entry documents, admission or parole, and any other INA benefit. Their visas/entry documents must be revoked regardless of issuance date, effective immediately and automatically canceling other valid visas/entry documents in their possession. The immigration sanctions also apply to each sanctioned foreign person's spouse, parent, sibling or adult child; the separate property-blocking requirement applies to the principal foreign persons described in 3(a)(1). Foreign person means someone other than the defined United States person, which includes U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents, U.S.-organized entities and any person in the United States. The incorporated INA alien definition excludes U.S. citizens and nationals. Protected persons include any defined U.S. person unless the United States both formally consents to ICC jurisdiction and is a Rome Statute party. They also include foreign citizens or lawful residents of a NATO or designated major non-NATO ally that has not consented to ICC jurisdiction or is not a Rome Statute party. The listed military/government personnel are inclusive examples, not the entire protected class. The President may waive sanctions case by case for periods no longer than 90 days each on a reported vital-national-security determination before the waiver takes effect, including the specified detailed rationale and actions by the United States and ICC. The President may terminate sanctions on written certification that the ICC has ceased all covered efforts and permanently closed/withdrawn/ended/terminated them. Imposition also requires congressional briefing/written notice within 10 days. The package includes property blocking under existing IEEPA authorities and penalties, rescission of available ICC appropriations at enactment and a prospective ban on using appropriated funds for the ICC. Immigration membership follows the direct travel/admission/parole/benefit restrictions, not the foreign-affairs findings. These are proposed legislative requirements; existing general INA inadmissibility/temporary-admission authorities are not treated as newly created by this bill. Actual designation, visa revocation, sanctions, enforcement or enactment is not inferred.

The exact House-passed H.R.30 adds INA 212(a)(2)(J) inadmissibility for a person convicted of, admitting commission of, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements of a sex offense under 34 USC 20911(5), or a conspiracy to commit one. New 212(a)(2)(K) uses those same conviction/admission predicates for a crime of domestic violence (defined through 237(a)(2)(E)), stalking, child abuse/neglect/abandonment, or a crime violating the protective-order portion addressing credible threats, repeated harassment or bodily injury. The INA baseline makes these inadmissibility grounds relevant to visas and admission; the bill is not limited by its title to persons unlawfully present. It separately adds INA 237(a)(2)(G) deportability for conviction of a defined sex offense or conspiracy: admission of conduct alone is not the predicate in this new deportability clause. The existing 237(a)(2)(E)(i) after-admission conviction ground for domestic violence, stalking and child abuse/neglect/abandonment remains; its domestic-violence definition is expanded to include any crime constituting domestic violence under 34 USC 12291(a), regardless of whether the jurisdiction receives grants. Noncriminal behavior mentioned in the victim-services portion of that definition is not itself converted into a crime by this bill. The incorporated sex-offense definition covers criminal sexual-act/contact offenses, specified offenses against minors, listed federal/military offenses, and attempts/conspiracies, with its foreign-conviction fairness and consensual-conduct limitations. The latter exclude specified consensual adult conduct unless custodial authority exists, and specified conduct where the victim is at least 13 and the offender is not more than 4 years older. Some covered conduct already can trigger existing criminal inadmissibility or deportability grounds; these are additional grounds and a definition expansion, not the creation of all immigration consequences for these crimes. INA 101(a)(48) supplies the existing conviction framework, including specified withheld adjudications with a guilt/plea/facts predicate plus court-ordered punishment, penalty or restraint. H.R.30 references 20911(5), rather than expressly importing the separate 20911(8) juvenile-conviction definition. The bill leaves the 237(a)(7) discretionary battered-person waiver for specified domestic-violence/stalking/protective-order deportability grounds intact; that waiver is not written to cover the new sex-offense ground. Existing 212(d)(3) discretionary temporary nonimmigrant admission and 212(d)(13)/(14) T/U status waiver authorities remain within their own conditions. Existing 212(h) enumerates other criminal grounds and is not expanded to the newJ/K grounds. No universal waiver or automatic removal is established.

S.5 would extend the federal mandatory-custody category to the following offenses: burglary, theft, larceny, shoplifting, assault of a law-enforcement officer, or any crime resulting in another person's death or serious bodily injury. The listed property-offense terms, assault of a law-enforcement officer and serious bodily injury take the meanings assigned by the jurisdiction where the acts occurred. The exact bill adds an INA 236(c) mandatory-custody category requiring inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(6)(A), (6)(C), or (7) together with a specified criminal predicate: being charged, arrested, convicted, admitting commission, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements. These inadmissibility categories concern presence without admission/parole or undesignated arrival, material immigration fraud/false citizenship claims, and specified entry-document defects, subject to their existing statutory qualifications. DHS must issue a detainer for a person meeting the new ground and, if the person is not otherwise detained by Federal, State or local officials, effectively and expeditiously take custody. The bill also gives a State attorney general or other authorized State officer standing, on alleged harm to the State or residents (including financial harm in excess of $100), to seek appropriate injunctive relief in district court over five specified federal matters: INA 235(b)(1)/(2) detention/removal requirements; INA 236 release, bond or parole decisions; the existing INA 243(d) visa-discontinuance requirement for countries denying or unreasonably delaying acceptance; violation of the existing INA 212(d)(5)(A) case-by-case urgent-humanitarian/significant-public-benefit parole limits; and INA 241(a)(2) detention during the removal period. Courts must advance and expedite these cases to the greatest practicable extent. INA 236(e) removes its express release/grant shield while leaving the other printed discretionary-judgment/detention/revocation/denial restrictions, and INA 242(f)(1) receives an exception for the printed listed actions, while its separate final-removal-order injunction standard remains. These review changes do not establish a general right to enjoin every immigration action. The parole clause changes its named administering actor to the Secretary of Homeland Security. The baseline removal period is generally 90 days with specified starting/extension conditions; the bill adds litigation standing over its detention requirement rather than creating that period. The pre-existing narrow witness/cooperator-protection release exception remains, redesignated as INA 236(c)(4).

The exact House-passed H.R.35 adds 18 USC 40B: operating a motor vehicle within 100 miles of the United States border while intentionally fleeing a pursuing U.S. Border Patrol agent acting under lawful authority, or a pursuing Federal/State/local officer actively assisting or under Border Patrol command. The ordinary penalty alternatives are imprisonment up to 2 years, a title 18 fine, or both; where serious bodily injury results the imprisonment alternative is 5–20 years, and where any person's death results it is 10 years to life, with fine-or-both alternatives retained in both cases. The bill adds INA 212(a)(2)(J) inadmissibility and 237(a)(2)(G) deportability for any alien convicted of, admitting commission of, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements of 40B(a). It also inserts 208A making a person meeting that same predicate ineligible for relief under the immigration laws, expressly including asylum under 208. Neither arrest alone nor merely being within 100 miles is the printed immigration predicate. Pre-existing 18 USC 758 already criminalizes vehicle flight/evasion from an immigration or other federal checkpoint followed by fleeing law-enforcement agents above the legal speed limit, with up-to 5 years/fine/both; existing 237(a)(2)(A)(iv) already makes a conviction for 758 deportable. H.R.35 creates a different officer/geography/intent predicate and additional immigration consequences, rather than the first-ever immigration checkpoint-flight offense or deportability ground. Unlike that existing deportability ground, the newG also accepts specified admissions. Existing INA 101(a)(48) conviction rules remain. The Attorney General, with the Secretary of Homeland Security, must report annually to both Judiciary Committees on violations, charged/apprehended/not-charged/not-apprehended counts, and penalties sought/imposed. A reporting duty is not evidence of actual violations, convictions or enforcement. The separate broad relief-bar clause is preserved as printed; it is not replaced by a blanket claim that existing narrow waivers guarantee relief, and no individual asylum or removal outcome is decided.

The exact H.R.495 EH proposal adds “and annually thereafter” to Public Law 117-263 section 7134(a)(2), after “development of the strategic plan”. The Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection would therefore report on implementation of the existing counter illicit cross-border tunnel operations strategic plan not later than one year after its development and annually thereafter, to the House Homeland Security and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committees. The pre-existing 7134(a)(1) already requires the Commissioner, coordinating with the DHS Science and Technology Under Secretary and appropriate DHS officials, to develop the plan within 180 days of the 2022law. Its existing scope includes risk-based identification/breach/assessment/remediation criteria, technologies and community impacts, information sharing, Border Patrol sector indicators and technology/staffing needs. H.R.495 changes the reporting cadence, not those plan requirements. The separate 6 USC 257 annual report on discovered Mexico–U.S. tunnels and DHS prevention/investigation/prosecution needs already exists and is not the provision amended here. Existing 7134(b) authorized$1 million for each of fiscal 2023 and 2024 for plan development and remediation; H.R.495 neither extends that authorization nor supplies new appropriations. Membership follows direct border-tunnel operations reporting. Actual reporting, tunnel remediation, border outcomes or enactment are not established by the House suspension-and-passage vote.

The exact H.R.993 EH proposal requires the DHS Secretary, acting through the CBP Commissioner and DHS Science and Technology Under Secretary, to submit a plan within 180 days of enactment to the House Homeland Security and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committees. The plan is to identify, integrate and deploy emerging/advanced technologies to enhance or address gaps in border-security operations. Its prescribed contents cover innovation-team use and composition, contributions and coordination, technologies from other agencies, procurement authorities and need for alternatives, scaling programs, program goals/timelines, border-community privacy/security impacts, replacement costs, research/private-sector coordination, metrics and listed aircraft/surveillance/inspection/tunnel/communications technologies. The bill gives the CBP Commissioner express authority to maintain one or more innovation teams to research and adapt new/emerging commercial technologies for border capability gaps and urgent mission needs, and assess potential outcomes including negative consequences where documented gaps are yet to be determined. It requires each maintained team to establish operating procedures, defined roles/partner relationships and transition protocols, plus strategic planning with costs, timeframes, metrics and performance parameters, including technology-transition rates. The Commissioner must report within 180 days and annually thereafter to the same committees on team procedures/plans, technologies piloted in the preceding fiscal year, success/gap determinations and status of transitioning successful technologies. This provides statutory authority and prescribed planning/reporting for maintaining teams; it does not establish that innovation teams or pilots first come into existence with this proposal. The technology list and planned deployment goals are not universal mandates to deploy every technology. No appropriation, universal pilot success or actual operational outcome is stated. Membership follows the express direct border-operations scope rather than DHS administration alone.

The exact H.R.2056 EH proposal prohibits the District of Columbia from having a statute, ordinance, policy or practice that prohibits or restricts a District government entity or official from sending, receiving, maintaining or exchanging information about any individual's citizenship or immigration status, lawful or unlawful, with any Federal, State or local government entity. It separately prohibits such District restrictions on compliance with a lawfully made DHS request under INA 236 or 287 to comply with a detainer for, or notify about release of, an individual. This is an express D.C.-specific restriction on governmental policies/practices. Existing 8 USC 1373 and 1644 already contain statutory restrictions on limiting certain status-information exchanges with the immigration service; the bill is not the first general permission to communicate immigration status. The bill's printed information clause includes citizenship as well as status and communication with any listed governmental entity, while its separate lawful-request clause specifically addresses detainers/release notices. INA 236 and 287 already govern qualified immigration custody and officer powers, including specified custody/release conditions, arrest limits and cooperation provisions. H.R.2056 does not itself rewrite those authorities, deem every DHS request lawful, or establish that every individual detainer must be obeyed. It bars District policies restricting the specified lawful-request compliance; individual custody legality, actual information disclosure/detention/removal, implementation and enactment are not inferred.

The exact H.R.875 EH proposal adds INA 212(a)(2)(J) inadmissibility for any alien convicted of, admitting commission of, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements of an intoxicated/impaired-driving offense. The terms take their meaning under the law of the jurisdiction where the conviction, offense or essential acts occurred, expressly including alcohol/drug influence or impairment, without regard to misdemeanor/felony classification under Federal, State, tribal or local law. Existing INA 212(a) makes inadmissibility relevant to visas and admission. It separately adds INA 237(a)(2)(G) deportability for conviction of a jurisdiction-defined intoxicated/impaired-driving offense, including alcohol/drug influence or impairment, regardless of the listed misdemeanor/felony classification. That clause uses the law where conviction occurred and does not make admission of conduct alone its predicate. Neither clause requires an injury/death or multiple offenses. The existing INA 101(a)(48) conviction framework remains, including specified withheld-adjudication situations with guilt/plea/facts and court-ordered punishment/penalty/restraint. These are additional categorical statutory grounds, rather than a claim that covered conduct previously could never trigger other criminal inadmissibility or deportability. Existing criminal INA grounds retain their own elements and exceptions. The single-offense minor/petty-offense exception in 212(a)(2)(A), the enumerated 212(h) waiver, and the 237(a)(2)(A)(vi) pardon exception are not printed exceptions to new J/G. Existing discretionary temporary-nonimmigrant/T/U inadmissibility waiver routes are retained within their own conditions; no categorical relief, guilt or automatic deportation is inferred. The bill concerns any alien meeting the grounds, not only a person unlawfully present.

The exact H.R.275 EH proposal requires the DHS Secretary, by the seventh day of each month starting with the first full month after enactment, to publish a DHS webpage report and submit it to the House Homeland Security and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committees. Each report must give the preceding month's total encounters of “special interest aliens”, their nationalities or countries of last habitual residence, geographic disaggregation, whether encounters occurred at land/air/sea ports of entry, between ports or in the U.S. interior, and identification of covered-nation nationalities/residences. The first report also covers January 20, 2021 through January 19, 2025. The operative definition is an INA-defined alien who, based on analysis of travel patterns, potentially poses a national-security risk to the United States or its interests. It does not establish an actual threat, criminal guilt, inadmissibility or removal for an individual. The incorporated covered nations are North Korea, China, Russia and Iran under 10 USC 4872(f)(2); only that definition is imported, not the unrelated procurement powers. The operative report covers DHS encounters, including the interior. The title's reference to attempts at unlawful entry does not create an unstated unlawful-entry-only reporting limit. This bill adds this specific recurring and retrospective reporting duty; it neither changes admission/removal eligibility nor authorizes new detention or spending. No actual report, encounter totals, threat finding or enactment is inferred.

The exact H.R.3486 EH proposal raises the INA 275(a) subsequent improper-entry offense imprisonment maximum from 2 to 5 years; the existing first-offense 6-month maximum/fine-or-both and other 275 provisions remain. New 275(e) covers an alien who enters/attempts entry at an undesignated time/place, eludes immigration examination/inspection, or attempts/obtains entry through willfully false/misleading representation or concealment of a material fact, and thereafter is convicted of a crime punishable by more than one year. That conjunction carries mandatory imprisonment of at least 5 years up to life, with an optional title 18 fine. Mere unlawful presence, arrest or all first entries do not alone satisfy it. INA 276(a) continues to require prior denial of admission/exclusion/deportation/removal or departure while a removal-type order is outstanding, followed by entry/attempt or being found in the United States. It raises the general maximum from 2 to 10 years, with fine-or-both alternatives. It preserves advance express consent to reapply and the specified prior-denial/removal no-advance-consent exception, naming DHS rather than the Attorney General. Rewritten 276(b), except where new(c) applies, raises the maximum for pre-removal conviction of at least 3 drug/person misdemeanors from 10 to 15 years. It retains the specified INA 235(c)/TitleV exclusion/removal unauthorized reentry category's 10-year nonconcurrent prison term plus fine, and the qualified 241(a)(4)(B) early-removal reentry category's 10-year maximum/fine-or-both. It adds a category for at least 3 prior denials/exclusions/deportations/removals followed by entry/attempt/being found, with 10-year maximum/fine-or-both. New 276(c) overrides(a)/(b) penalties for a covered reentrant convicted before removal/departure of an aggravated felony, any crime classed as a felony by the relevant Federal/State/Tribal/local jurisdiction, or any crime punishable by more than one year: mandatory imprisonment of at least 10 years up to life, with an optional fine. This replaces the prior felony/aggravated-felony maximums rather than changing every felony into an INA aggravated felony. The existing INA aggravated-felony definition and its offense-specific/foreign-offense qualifications remain. Stipulated-removal agreements during or outside Federal/State criminal trials count as removal for(b)/(c). The existing remainder-of-unserved-sentence reentry provision is redesignated(d), with its removal cross-reference and administering actor updated. Existing collateral attack on the underlying order remains redesignated(e), requiring exhaustion of available administrative remedies, improper deprivation of judicial review and fundamental unfairness. These are legislative penalty/actor/cross-reference changes; individual guilt, validity of a removal order, sentence, actual enforcement or enactment is not inferred.

The exact H.R.4638 EH proposal adds INA 212(a)(2)(J) inadmissibility and 237(a)(2)(G) deportability for an alien convicted of, admitting commission of, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements of an offense under 18 USC 1368. Both new clauses allow those specified admissions, despite the conviction-only phrasing in the bill title. Arrest alone is not the printed predicate. The incorporated 1368 offense already criminalizes willfully and maliciously harming a police animal, including attempts and conspiracies. Police animal means a dog or horse employed by a Federal agency in any branch primarily to aid criminal detection, law enforcement or apprehension. It is not every working animal or every State/local police animal, and the bill is not limited to CBP animals. The existing offense carries fine and up-to 1year imprisonment, with up-to 10 years for permanent disability/disfigurement, serious bodily injury or death; the immigration clauses do not add an injury/penalty-length threshold. The bill adds INA consequences to that existing crime, not a new animal-harm offense or a claim that all covered conduct previously had no immigration consequences. Existing INA conviction rules/other criminal grounds remain. Their enumerated petty-offense,212(h) and pardon exceptions are not written as exceptions to newJ/G; discretionary temporary-admission/T/U waiver authorities remain within their own scope. No blanket relief or automatic deportation is inferred.

The exact H.R.1689 EH proposal directs the Secretary of Homeland Security, notwithstanding any other law, to designate Haiti for temporary protected status until the date three months after January 20,2029—April 20,2029. It is a mandatory country-specific designation for that stated duration rather than a newly created TPS program or a direction to apply only ordinary discretionary six-to-eighteen-month designation periods. It does not state that Haiti has never before been designated or resolve litigation/agency decisions about earlier designations. The pre-existing 8 USC 1254a framework distinguishes designation of a country from granting TPS to an individual national (or stateless person last habitually resident there). Individual eligibility requires continuous U.S. physical presence since the effective date of the most recent designation, residence since the designated date, registration, applicable admissibility and absence of statutory bars, with stated brief/casual/innocent absence and emergency-trip qualifications. The bill does not supply individual presence/residence/registration dates or remove these requirements. Existing bars include a U.S.-committed felony or at least two misdemeanors and the incorporated persecution, particularly serious crime, serious nonpolitical foreign crime, security/terrorism and firm-resettlement grounds. Existing admissibility exceptions and individual humanitarian/family-unity/public-interest waivers retain their specified nonwaivable criminal/security boundaries. TPS may be withdrawn for ineligibility, disqualifying absence or registration failure without good cause. For a person granted TPS, the existing framework supplies protection from removal during the status period and employment authorization; it does not itself grant permanent residence or citizenship, guarantee all public benefits or authorize a person abroad to enter to apply. Its status-based detention protection, consent-based travel and adjustment-status provisions keep their own limits. This bill imposes the country-duration mandate, not individual awards or actual implementation, removals, benefit outcomes or enactment.
